newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Peters says high NZ dlr a concern for exporters.
newsitem.headline: Peters says high NZ dlr a concern for exporters.

text.p: Treasurer Winston Peters said on Thursday the high level of the New Zealand dollar was still a concern to exporters.
"It would be wrong not be concerned of the affect on exporters," he told a news conference called to discuss Treasury's post-election briefing papers.

Asked if he expected the Reserve Bank to target anything other than price stability, Peters said: "You'll get no response to that today," but added that he would prefer to give a fuller answer to the question in the New Year.

The National-New Zealand First coalition agreed to widen the 0-2 percent inflation target to 0-3 percent and added that price stability would be maintained so monetary policy could make its maximum contribution to sustainable economic growth, employment and development opportunities.

"You will see from the PTA (Policy Target Agreement) ... that there is an acceptance of the need for sustainable growth. At that time sustainability and growth were concepts we put central to our coalition talks and that remains the case," Peters said.
"You have to more carefully examine what were carefully prepared words on behalf of the government. These are early days," Peters said.
He said the PTA change was released before ministers were sworn in.
Asked how he would lower the dollar he said he was not going to make off-the-cuff remarks that would push the dollar around.
He said when he had had more time in the job he would comment, adding he would do his very best to help exporters.
Asked about Treasury recommendations of further asset sales, Peters said that had long been Treasury's ideological position.
"That is a view that will have to have a view to the sentiments expressed very clearly in the coalition agreement on such state assets," Peters said.
The coalition document rules out the sale of large state assets, but does not place a blanket ban on them, although that was the policy of NZ First going into the October 12 election.

Asked about criticisms of the affordability of the coalition's programme by opposition deputy leader Michael Cullen and Bankers Trust chief economist David Plank, Peters said: "If you have regard to the deferral of taxes, over and above that there is not significant expenditure. I don't recall Bankers Trust arguing against the tax reduction predicated for July 1, 1997.
"I think you will always get a conservative call... but we are confident we have put together a very prudent expenditure programme and I think the market has welcomed it in that way.

"If the figures are accurate that we have been given then we have got the confidence to believe our policies can be implemented at the same time as going into the out years with debt reduction that will hit the 18.7 percent level."
He said the responsibilities of himself as Treasurer and Finance Minister Bill Birch would be worked through over time and the two intended to cooperate as much as possible.
"Overall tax strategy is the Treasurer's job. Implementation and collection is the minister of finance's job."
Along with the high dollar he said upskilling of the workforce and unemployment were concerns.
He said his advice to business would be to "hold on a little longer until you get a clear fix on the shape and framework and character of the new government".
Returning to the effects of monetary policy, Peters said he wanted to research the background assumptions being made.

"For example the effect of the minimum wage. What numbers does it affect? Is it an area in which they have had too much consideration? We would like to know what definitive work is behind that assumption," Peters said.
The RBNZ has said the coalition's plan to lift the adult minmium wage to $7 an hour would add to inflationary pressure.
